1.pericope_label: Idolatry forbidden, and the sabbaths and sanctuary to be reverenced

schools.summary: Gill reports the rabbinic view that the law is placed here for the sake of the Israelite sold to a heathen, prefers to treat it as a principal command in its own right, and glosses idols as things of nought while extending the graven image to the molten kind worked afterwards with a tool.

Henry likens the placing to a master repeating his weightiest charges last, explains why images above all provoke a God who is an infinite Spirit, observes that no sin was more provoking and none they were more addicted to, makes sabbaths and sanctuary the instrumental part of religion, and contrasts human law enforced by penalty with a God known as the rewarder of those who seek him.

Clarke traces the prohibition of pillars to the later abuse of stones anointed by holy men, as happened to the brazen serpent; Wesley limits the ban to pillars meant for worship, since holy men raised them before and after this law, and defines the reverence owed the sanctuary.

Ellicott protests that the chapter division severs these verses from the section they belong to and obscures their point, distinguishes the image, the pillar and the figured stone, and reports the second Temple's reading of the last as a paving stone lawful in the sanctuary and forbidden outside it; Keil and Delitzsch set the chapter against the close of the book of the covenant, the one promising conquest and the other continued possession.

debates: Whether these verses close the preceding section or open the chapter of blessing and curse
outliers: Ellicott judges the received chapter division to obscure both the sequence and the import of these verses

schools.summary: Gill reads the statutes as moral, ceremonial and judicial together, notes the plural your rains, dates threshing from March and vintage from July, and takes the promised peace of freedom from civil broils; Calvin concedes that the condition would be ineffectual if God examined works strictly, answers that faith hides the believer's defects, argues that the confining of reward to this life is elementary instruction, raises the difficulty that peace and the chasing of enemies do not agree, and finds the hope of immortality in the words I will be your God.

Clarke identifies the early and latter rain from Calmet, sets the Judaean agricultural calendar beside the Egyptian from Pliny, quotes Dodd on the entireness of the plenty, and takes the tabernacle promise for the gospel dispensation on the strength of John's word for tabernacling; Wesley draws the moral that God gave them a rain-fed and not a river-fed land to bind them to obedience, glosses five as a certain number for an uncertain, and reads the walking of the pillar of cloud and fire.

Ellicott argues that the Hebrew section and the English chapter both ought to begin at this verse, dates the early and vernal rains, complains that the Authorised Version renders the same Hebrew about evil beasts differently here and in Ezekiel, calls the five and the hundred proverbial, and explains the broken yoke-bands from Eastern ox harness; Keil and Delitzsch take lying down unafraid from a flock at rest, hear satisfied repose in the word for dwelling, and deny that God's walking refers to the journeys.

debates: Whether God's walking among them means his leading them on their journeys, as Gill and Wesley take it, or his presence with them in Canaan itself, as Keil and Delitzsch insist
How the promise of peace agrees with the promise of successful war, a difficulty Calvin alone raises
outliers: Calvin devotes much of his comment to refuting those who infer a changed divine nature, or two different Gods, from the absence of visible temporal judgments under the gospel

14.pericope_label: The first degree of judgment upon contempt of the law

schools.summary: Gill grades the offence from negligent hearing through non-performance to open contempt, and reads the setting of God's face as the exerting of his power against them, the reverse of the respect promised above; Calvin explains why threats are joined to a law meant to be obeyed willingly, answers the objection that fear cannot produce love, and narrows the description to deliberate apostates while conceding that all transgressors fall under the curse.

Henry excludes sins of ignorance and infirmity and of repentance, traces the descent from carelessness through contempt and abhorrence to the disowning of the covenant, observes that God made the covenant and man breaks it so that God has all the honour and man all the blame, takes appoint over you of taskmasters ruling with rigour, cites bishop Patrick on the falling sickness, and finds it just that those who would not have God reign should be ruled by those who hate them.

Clarke halts at these verses to expound twelve scriptural terms for the divine law from their Hebrew roots, sees the threatened evils personified as governors set over the people, and challenges the deist to compare the chapter with Jewish history since Vespasian; Wesley reads the breach of covenant as discharging God from the blessings promised on his part, and divides chronic from acute diseases in the same words Henry uses.

Ellicott marks the turn from promise to calamity and bounds the first degree of punishment at verse seventeen, finds the apostasy developing from passive indifference into contempt, would drop the adversative before the breaking of the covenant, and presses smitten for slain, rule for reign, and extinguish the eyes for consume the eyes; Keil and Delitzsch insist the judgments answer contempt of all the laws rather than single breaches, and read the terror as a general notion particularized as disease, fruitless sowing, defeat and flight.

debates: Whether the despising and abhorring described here reach only deliberate apostates, as Calvin holds, or lie at the end of a slope that begins in ordinary neglect, as Gill, Henry and Ellicott read it
outliers: Clarke suspends the exposition for a twelve-part lexical study of the words for law, taking the occasion of statutes and judgments standing together

18.pericope_label: The second, third and fourth stages of chastisement

schools.summary: Gill reports the rabbinic reading of the pride of power as the sanctuary while preferring the land and the forces, offers both the hostile and the accidental sense of walking contrary and applies the same ambiguity to God's side, allows the wild beasts to be literal or the monarchs of Assyria and Babylon, and takes the broken staff of a famine; Calvin reads the gradation itself as mercy, takes the sevenfold as an indefinite amplification, argues at length from the root that walking contrary means walking at adventures and ascribing adversity to fortune, insists that all wars are stirred at God's command, and stands alone in reading the ten women at one oven as abundance without satisfaction rather than scarcity.

Clarke collects the historical fulfilments of the wild beasts and quotes Ainsworth for their spiritual sense as tyrants and false prophets, and explains the ten women from the public bakehouses of the East as a mark of desolation and want; Wesley includes the ark and sanctuary in the pride of their power, glosses the quarrel of the covenant as God's quarrel with them for breaking it, and reads the ten women as many families weighing out what each put in.

Ellicott numbers the degrees of punishment and marks where each begins and ends, takes the sevenfold as an indefinite large number, reports the second Temple's reading of the pride of power as the sanctuary and twice complains that the Authorised Version obliterates the identity of phrases repeated in Deuteronomy, notes the reversal of the metals there, and reads the ten women and the bread by weight beside Ezekiel; Keil and Delitzsch stage the judgments, take seven as the number of perfection carried to full measure, define the pride of strength as all a nation rests its might upon, and add that the highways would cease for want of travellers.

debates: Whether the ten women baking at one oven signify scarcity, as Clarke, Wesley, Ellicott and the usual view have it, or abundance without nourishment, as Calvin argues from the breaking of the staff
Whether the word rendered contrary means hostile encounter, as Jerome, the Chaldee, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch take it, or accidental occurrence and walking at adventures, as Calvin prefers
Whether the pride of their power is the sanctuary, as the second Temple authorities and Wesley held, or the land and the armed forces, as Gill and Keil and Delitzsch prefer
outliers: Calvin reports Kitto's alternative, that ten households clubbed their dough together and divided the baked cakes by weight in proportion to what each contributed
Henry has no block keyed within this range; his exposition of the whole curse section stands at verse fourteen and is used in the entry there.

27.pericope_label: The final stage: desolation, dispersion, and the sabbaths of the land

schools.summary: Gill collects the historical instances of parents eating their children, reports Jarchi and Aben Ezra on the high places, reads the scattering as winnowing with a fan, describes the survivors falling over one another while rejecting the rabbinic reading that each falls for his brother's guilt, and passes on Rabbi Akiba's application of the loss among the heathen to the ten tribes; Calvin gathers from the cannibalism how terrible it is to fall into God's hands, takes the carcases cast on the idols as God's finger pointing at his abhorrence of their worship, explains why the land was joined with man in the sabbath and why an extorted rest was substituted for the voluntary one, and judges the lingering terror of the survivors more wretched than a swift death.

Clarke gives Josephus on the woman Mary at the siege of Jerusalem, reports Houbigant's computation that the seventy years of captivity exactly repaid the seventy sabbaths of years owed from Saul onward and infers that the sabbatical law was kept until then, and asks whether the losing of the people among the heathen refers to the ten tribes; Wesley points to Lamentations in a line, explains why the idols are called carcases, and presses the possessive in your sanctuaries as God's disowning of what they had defiled.

Ellicott bounds the fifth warning, notes the addition of in fury and the change of verb, argues from the context that the high places are idolatrous and renders the images as sun-pillars, marks the shift from invasions permitted to desolation wrought by God himself, observes the exact reversal of the promised immunity from the sword, prefers be lost to perish and because of their iniquity to in it, and cites the Chaldee on the fathers' sins held fast in their hands; Keil and Delitzsch deny that the land owed any sabbath debt and take the verb of enjoying rest against Gesenius and Knobel.

debates: Whether the land's rest repays a debt of sabbaths withheld, as Ellicott, Clarke and Calvin all assume, or whether the land was never under the obligation and merely enjoys rest, as Keil and Delitzsch argue against Gesenius and Knobel
Whether being lost among the heathen describes the ten tribes specifically, as Rabbi Akiba held and Clarke half suspects, or the nation at large, which Ellicott's remnant argument requires
Whether the high places are idolatrous shrines, towers and palaces, or places of sacrifice generally
outliers: Clarke rests a chronological argument on the exile, reasoning backwards from its seventy years to conclude that the sabbatical year had been observed down to Saul's reign
Henry has no block keyed within this range; his exposition of the whole curse section stands at verse fourteen and is used in the entry there.

40.pericope_label: Confession, the remembered covenant, and the close of the legislation

schools.summary: Gill prefers to read the confession as prediction rather than condition, notes the Targum's addition that it comes in the time of their distress, and refers the closing formula to the whole book; Calvin holds that mercy is offered to the very worst by the special privilege of the covenant, likens the fallen to shipwrecked sailors seizing a plank, distinguishes the confession meant from auricular confession under the papacy, warns that following the fathers makes a child less excusable rather than more, rejects both the patient-endurance and the glad-acceptance readings of accepting punishment in favour of a desire to appease God, and insists that for their sakes means for their profit and not their merit.

Henry reads the close as gracious promise, calls to the prisoners of hope, sets out three marks of repentance in confession, godly sorrow and submission, requires that they confess the wrath as well as the sin and overlook the second causes, explains why the unhumbled heart is called uncircumcised, accounts for the inverted order of the patriarchs as an ascending line back to the father of the faithful, and ends on the law as the bond of communion drawn with the cords of a man.

Ellicott reads the verse as prediction rather than condition, explains that the fathers are confessed for because they have perished and cannot confess themselves, renders accepting punishment as accepting willingly on the strength of the same verb rendered enjoy of the land's sabbaths, takes remember in the sense of perform, reports the second Temple's inference of three distinct covenants from the repetition of the word and the Chaldee's location of each, notes the solitary inversion of the patriarchs' order, and confines the closing formula to the section begun in the previous chapter; Keil and Delitzsch set out the construction joining confession to the remembering of the covenant and make the formula close the whole covenant legislation from Exodus onward.

Clarke observes that providence has kept the nation distinct and numerous through the fulfilled threatenings and looks for all Israel to be saved in one fold with the Gentiles, and conjectures that the following chapter once stood before this one, a column of the parchment roll having been displaced; Wesley glosses the uncircumcised heart as carnal and impenitent, reads accepting the punishment as patient submission with David, reports the comfort the Jews take from the promise and Paul's use of such passages, and repeats Henry's closing sentence on the law as a covenant almost word for word.

debates: What accepting the punishment of their iniquity means: willing and even glad acceptance, as Ellicott argues from the verb rendered enjoy; patient submission, as Wesley takes it; or the desire to appease God and atone, as Calvin prefers

How far the closing formula reaches, over the whole book as Gill and Clarke take it, over the section begun in the previous chapter as Ellicott argues, or over the covenant legislation from Exodus onward as Keil and Delitzsch hold
Whether the confession is a condition offered or a future predicted
outliers: Clarke explains the double conclusion of Leviticus by a physical accident, supposing a column of the parchment roll displaced so that the last chapter fell out of its original order
